full_judgment:
12. This jurisdictional aspect was argued mainly on the proclamation of Martial Law dated 20th August, 1975. Mr. Serajul Huq has placed the entire proclamation of 20th August, 1975 and canvassed that the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has continued to remain in force subject to the proclamation and Martial Law Regulation and Orders. In clause (g) the jurisdiction of the superior Courts has been ousted on a very limited ground, namely (i) the Court shall have no power to question in any manner whatsoever or declare illegal or void the Proclamation or any Martial Law Regulation or Order; (ii) nor any order made under the Proclamation or action taken or anything done under the Proclamation are liable to be challenged, Mr. Huq has argued that unlike Martial Law of 1958 which was proclaimed by Md. Ayub Khan and the Martial Law of 1969 of General Yahya Khan the Constitution was not abrogated by the Proclamation of 20th August, 1975. The jurisdiction of the superior Courts have been curtailed for specific purpose with limited objective because the consideration of Martial Law is that the "security, peace and progress, prosperity and development of the country" and for paving the way for general election, vide Proclamation dated 8th November, 1975 which is to be read with deeming clause "to be a part of the Proclamation of the 20th August, 1975". Mr. Huq has argued if this is the overt policy of Proclamation of Martial Law which was done by the Proclaimed on 20th August, 1975 while seizing the full power of the Government with the help and mercy of the Almighty Allah and relying upon blessings of the people the authority Who is to discharge the functions of Martial Law cannot act in a manner which is a negation of it. Since jurisdiction of the superior Court is to determine the question between the litigating public in accordance with law this function has been saddled upon the Judges of this Court for achieving the end of law which is human happiness. Therefore, it is argued that the Martial Law which was proclaimed for establishing peace, order, security, progress and prosperity has no reason to curtail the jurisdiction of the superior Courts. 

 13. By the Charter of 1774 the Supreme Court was established in Bengal and the Judges of that Court had been assigned by clause 4 the powers, functions of Kings Bench Division. When the High Court Act of 1861 was passed functions and power was preserved by section 9. Letters Patent of 1865 declared that the High Court is a Court of record and empowered to punish for contempt. Government of India Act, 1919 by section 106 preserved all the jurisdiction of the High Court and the same was retained in Government of India Act, 1935. When the India Independence Act 1947 was passed and two Dominions were created, Government of India Act, 1935 continued till the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. High Court was established by Article 165 and writ jurisdiction was conferred by Article 170. By Article 224 Letters Patent constituting the High Court was declared as "existing law" and by Article 227(5) it was stipulated that the High Court will have the same jurisdiction and power as it had before the Constitution day. 

 15. This power continued, till 7-10-58 when the Constitution was abrogated by Md. Ayub Khan. By Continuance of Laws Order 1958 post proclamation order that jurisdiction was retained subject to proclamation of Martial Law and its regulation. Challenge was given before the Supreme Court as to whether the superior Courts could call in question the grievances, the propriety or finding and legality of the order passed by Military Court. In the case of Ayub khan reported in P.L.D. 1960 (SC) 237. Munir. C.J. declared that the jurisdiction of the Court exists. In that case the Supreme Court of Pakistan quashed the conviction. 

 17. This Constitution of 1962 was abrogated in 1969 when the Martial Law was promulgated. But the power of the Court was preserved in Article 5(b) subject to the condition that the Court will not call into question the proclamation of Martial Law and no writ could be passed against the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Again, the question was raised as to the jurisdictional aspect. Lahore High Court in a Full Bench decision in the case of Mir Hasan, reported in PLD 1969 Lahore, 786 declared that this power of the Court cannot be taken away. No appeal was filed against that decision. However to notify the decision the Government attempted a device by way of passing a. Martial Law Order being Martial Law Order No. 3 of 1969. The Supreme Court declared that that Martial Law Order No. 3 of 1969 was illegal in Asma Jilani PLD 1972 (SC) 139. Hence the debate as to the jurisdiction of the superior Courts though continued the trend of decision shows that the jurisdiction was not only claimed but was exercised. 

 40. Now the Regulation 3 empowers the Government to transfer a case from one Court to another Martial Law Court or from a Criminal Court or Special Tribunal to a Martial Law Court. The Notification reads thus:- 

 No. 991-JIV/2T-17/76-In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the Martial' Law Regulations, 1975, the Government is pleased to transfer the cases mentioned in column 1 of the Schedule below and pending in the Courts shown in column II thereof to the Special Martial Law Courts specified in column III of the Schedule: 

 44. When the Court was constituted by Regulation I no special Court or tribunal was mentioned. Regulation 2 provides that the Government may by notification in the official gazette, constitute special martial law Courts and summary martial law Courts for such areas as may be specified in the notification. The marginal notes mentions "Martial Law Courts" although in the proclamation it has mentioned only "Special Courts or Tribunals". In the previous two Martial Laws in 1958 and 1969 when the Constitution was abrogated Special Courts were created, namely. Special Military Court and Summary Military Court and these were legal conceptions known to law. But the conception of Martial Law Court is something new which is not found in Army Act or any other enactment. In the Proclamation of 1969 the power was reserved for providing for setting up Military Court. By regulation 2 special Court of criminal jurisdiction were created, namely, Special Military Court and Summary Military Court. But it was provided that this Special Military Court should be constituted in the same manner and should exercise the same powers and should follow the same procedure as a Field General Court Martial convened under the Pakistan Army Act, 1952 and the provisions of that Act and of the Rules made thereunder should apply to and govern all such proceedings. 

 “Government may transfer a case from one Martial Law Court to another Martial Law Court or from a Criminal Court or Special Tribunal to Martial Law Court.” 

 No attempt was made as to which of the cases are to be tried by ordinary Court or which cases are liable to be transferred to. Martial Law Court. The learned Deputy Attorney General could not show any Regulation or Order which has laid down the guide-line or classified the cases to be tried by the respective Courts. Government has the power to set up Special Court and this is not disputed. Once a Special Court is established it is at once the duty to supply the norm as to how concurrence of the jurisdiction are to be regulated. This was noticed by Munir, C J. in the case of Ayub Khuro thus: 

 48. The charge-sheet was submitted and the case was pending before the Special Tribusunal, Mymensingh. The case transferred to the Martial Law Court which was not declared by law to be a Court of Special jurisdiction nor any class of cases were allotted to it. Alternatively if the two have concurrent jurisdiction, if at all, in the matters of crime under ordinary law the one which was created especially for trying these cases, namely, Special Tribunal, cannot be divested from its jurisdiction by mere order of a transfer passed in the executive jurisdiction. This view was also accepted in the case of Mr. Hassan Vs. State, reported in PLD 1969 Lahore. 786 where it was noted that the Special Judge appointed under the Pakistan Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958, is a Court of special jurisdiction, its jurisdiction being confined only to specific class of cases under a prescribed procedure. Martial Law Regulation No. 42, therefore, would not be attracted to this category of Cases pending in the Court of Special Judge. Accordingly the Full Bench held that the order transferring the case from the Court of the Special Judge to the Special Military Court was defective on the legal plane and was without jurisdiction. 

 “All proceedings of Special Martial Law Courts shall immediately after the termination thereof to be submitted to the Government for review and all sentences of death or transportation for life shall have to be confirmed by the President.” 

 (1) it means in the first place the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power and excludes the existence of arbitrariness of prerogative or even of wide discretionary authority on the part of the government; 

 "As I have said already, in the present case the discrimination arises on the terms of the Act itself. The fact that it gives unrestrained power to the State Government to select in any way it likes the particular cases of offences which should go to a Special Tribunal and withdraw in such cases the protection which the accused normally enjoys under the criminal Law of the country, is on the face of it discriminatory” 

 73. Martial Law Regulation No.16 of 1976 dated 14-16-76 has provides for jurisdiction of special Martial Law tribunal. Sub-clause (4) says the tribunal may try any offence, whether committed before or after the commencement of this Regulation punishable (a) under chapter-VI or VII of the Penal Code, (b) under the Army Act, the Air Force Act, he Nevy ordinance or any other Rules or Regulations made thereunder, (c) under Regulations 13 or 17 of the Martial Law Regulations (d) attempts or conspires to commit or abetment of etc. and also provided that the tribunal may also try such other offences punishable under any other Martial Law Regulation or law for the time being in force as the Government may, by order in writing, direct. Thus a classification has been made and whenever retrospectivity has been given it has been said so expressly even by the Martial Law Regulation. Therefore, it is laic in the day to argue (hat the enabling power given under Martial Law Regulation 2(3) provides for transfer of cases from ordinary criminal Court to Martial Law Court only because an order has been passed by the Government in respect of offence committed before the Martial Law. In this connection section 94 of the Army Act 1952 may be considered which contemplates a case of concurrent jurisdiction of a criminal Court and a Court martial in respect of "civil offence" and section 95 provides that if the criminal Court is of the opinion that the proceedings ought to 'have been instituted before it in respect of "civil offence" then the controversy can be resolved by referring the matter to the Central Government whose order upon such reference is final. No such provision has been made by the Proclamation or Regulation. 

 74. We have already found that present Martial Law is completely different from that of 1958 or 1969. The constitution has not been abrogated; only certain part of it has been circumscribed by the Martial Law Proclamation out of necessity. This Martial Law is a mere constitutional deviation and not one of Wellingtonian style. The Chief Justice of Bangladesh, instead of the Speaker, had to administer oath to the President after proclamation of Martial Law. Not only that the Chief Justice had to perform the task of both President and Chief Martial Law. Administrator for some time until the office of the Chief Martial Law Administrator was handed over to the Army Chief. The Martial Law Courts had been set up to try certain specific offences and certain now offences as was created by Martial Law Regulations. The function and jurisdiction of the normal Courts were not disturbed. Remedial measures were taken by amendment of Emergency Powers Act and Special Powers Act; provisions of bail were free from restrictive conditions. Thus on the Whole, the declared policy to take the county to the cherished goal through democracy was being pursued. In such setting, the contention that jurisdiction of the superior Court has been ousted in so far as Martial Law Courts are concerned do not appear to be sound Moreover, in this trial five accused had been sentenced to death by a Tribunal which was not composed by persons having judicial experience in civil offence. Without mean in any disrespect, the Martial Law Court has purported to try an ordinary penal offence of murder punishable under section 302 BPC The offence was not one of those Military offences. It was a simple "civil offence". To deny an appeal from such conviction is to treat discriminately. In such situation the judicial power of the superior Court is all the more attracted to examine whether the trial was held in the exercise of jurisdiction. Viewing the matter from this angle, we have come to the conclusion that the transfer itself was defective and illegal. It was a case pending before Special Tribunal. Had it been the case that the Martial Law Regulations have provided that all the cases under suction 302 BPC are triable by Special Martial Law, then possibly an argument would be advanced in support of the proposition that this petition is not maintainable.
